subject: anaesthesia
title: Specialty Anaesthesia: Neuroanaesthesia, Oculocardiac Reflex, and Laser Airway Safety

steps.title: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure Dynamics
steps.tx: **Cerebral perfusion pressure calculation** is defined by the formula: CPP equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus intracranial pressure (ICP), or central venous pressure (CVP) if higher than ICP. Normal adult resting CPP is 70 to 90 mmHg; maintaining CPP strictly above 60 to 70 mmHg prevents focal cerebral ischemia, while cerebral autoregulation maintains constant cerebral blood flow (approx 50 mL/100g/min) across MAP limits of 50 to 150 mmHg.

rows: Titrate with vasopressors if ICP elevated

steps.title: Intracranial Pressure Control Strategies
steps.tx: **Medical management of raised intracranial pressure** employs multiple synergistic modalities: elevate the head of the bed 30 degrees (facilitating venous drainage without kinking internal jugular veins), administer osmotic diuretic mannitol (0.5 to 1.0 g/kg IV) or 3 percent hypertonic saline, maintain normothermia, ensure deep neuromuscular relaxation, and induce temporary mild hyperventilation to a PaCO2 of 30 to 35 mmHg.

nodes.label: Elevate head 30 degrees and maintain neutral neck alignment
Infuse IV mannitol (0.5 to 1.0 g/kg) or 3% hypertonic saline bolus
Hyperventilate temporarily to PaCO2 30 to 35 mmHg
Deepen anaesthesia with propofol to suppress metabolic CMRO2

steps.title: Carbon Dioxide Vasoreactivity
steps.tx: **Cerebral vascular reactivity to carbon dioxide** causes marked changes in cerebral blood flow: for every 1 mmHg change in arterial PaCO2 between 20 and 60 mmHg, cerebral blood flow shifts linearly by approximately 1 to 2 mL/100g/min (or 3 to 4 percent). Acute hyperventilation to PaCO2 30 to 35 mmHg causes arteriolar vasoconstriction, shrinking cerebral blood volume and slackening a tense brain, but prolonged severe hypocapnia (<25 mmHg) induces cerebral ischemia.

left.title: Controlled Mild Hyperventilation (PaCO2 30-35)
points: Arteriolar cerebral vasoconstriction reduces cerebral blood volume
Provides immediate slack, relaxed brain for surgical exposure
Preserves adequate neuronal microvascular oxygen delivery

right.title: Severe Excessive Hypocapnia (PaCO2 <25)
points: Shifts oxyhaemoglobin curve left, impairing tissue oxygen release
Triggers secondary cytotoxic ischaemic neuronal necrosis

steps.title: The Oculocardiac Reflex (Aschner Reflex)
steps.tx: **Oculocardiac reflex trigeminovagal pathway** (Aschner phenomenon) is triggered during ophthalmic surgery by traction on extraocular rectus muscles (medial rectus traction is most potent), pressure on the globe, or retrobulbar hematoma. The afferent pathway travels via ciliary nerves, ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V1), and Gasserian ganglion to the main sensory trigeminal nucleus in the brainstem.

rows: Stretch receptors in muscle belly and tendon
Most potent with medial rectus traction
Long/short ciliary nerves to CN V1 (ophthalmic)
Conducts sensory impulse to trigeminal nucleus
Blocked by effective retrobulbar/peribulbar local block
Premedicate with IV atropine or glycopyrrolate
Immediately tell surgeon to release muscle traction

steps.tx: Trace the wiring in this diagram and a tug on an eye muscle ends at the heart. Afferent fibres ride the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve into the brainstem, cross to the vagus, and return as a **trigeminovagal reflex** that can slow the heart to a standstill. Children under strabismus surgery fire it most readily, medial rectus traction pulling hardest. The treatment choreography is rehearsed: stop the stimulus, deepen anaesthesia, and give atropine if the bradycardia refuses to lift.
steps.say: The oculocardiac reflex runs from trigeminal V1 to vagus X, slowing the heart when eye muscles are pulled.

steps.title: Management of Oculocardiac Reflex
steps.tx: **Emergency management of oculocardiac bradycardia** requires instant communication: immediately instruct the surgeon to release all traction on the extraocular muscle. Traction release typically restores normal sinus rhythm within seconds; if severe bradycardia or asystole persists despite cessation of traction, administer intravenous atropine (0.02 mg/kg) or glycopyrrolate, verify adequate depth of anaesthesia, and confirm normoxaemia.

nodes.label: Sudden bradycardia or asystole during strabismus surgery
Tell ophthalmic surgeon loudly to 'Release muscle traction immediately'
Verify prompt return of normal sinus rhythm upon release
Administer IV atropine (0.02 mg/kg) if bradycardia persists

steps.title: Laser Airway Surgery Fire Safety
steps.tx: **Laser airway surgery fire hazards** occur when carbon dioxide or Nd:YAG lasers ignite endotracheal tubes in an oxygen-enriched surgical field. Standard polyvinyl chloride tubes ignite and burn vigorously, generating toxic hydrochloric acid fumes. Laser safety mandates specialized laser-resistant metallic tubes (flexible stainless steel or copper-wrapped), filling the tube cuff with saline tinted with methylene blue, and reducing inspired oxygen concentration (FIO2) under 30 percent in helium or nitrogen.

rows: Reflects laser beam; prevents shaft puncture
Never use standard polyvinyl chloride tubes
Saline tinted with methylene blue dye
Extinguishes laser beam if cuff punctured
Blue dye leak instantly alerts surgeon to cuff breach
Halt ventilation; pull tube; flood with saline
Removes oxidizer, fuel, and heat source
Ventilate with mask and re-intubate to assess damage

steps.title: Airway Fire Extinguishment Protocol
steps.tx: **Emergency airway fire protocol** demands immediate memorized execution: instantly halt ventilation and disconnect the breathing circuit (removing oxygen fuel), immediately extubate the burning endotracheal tube from the patient, and pour cold sterile saline down the airway to extinguish residual smoldering embers. Subsequently, ventilate via mask with 100 percent oxygen, reintubate, and perform rigid bronchoscopy to assess mucosal thermal damage.

nodes.label: Disconnect breathing circuit from endotracheal tube immediately
Pull burning endotracheal tube from trachea and discard in bucket
Instill cold sterile saline down pharynx and trachea
Ventilate with 100% O2 via mask, re-intubate, and inspect via bronchoscopy

steps.title: Laparoscopic Pneumoperitoneum Hemodynamics
steps.tx: **Laparoscopic carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum** (insufflation pressure maintained at 12 to 15 mmHg) alters cardiopulmonary mechanics: elevated intra-abdominal pressure compresses the inferior vena cava (dropping venous return and cardiac output), pushes the diaphragm cephalad (reducing functional residual capacity, promoting basal atelectasis, and escalating peak airway pressures), and absorbs carbon dioxide across the peritoneal membrane, causing hypercapnia that demands a 20 to 30 percent increase in minute ventilation.

left.title: Cardiovascular Consequences
points: Elevated intra-abdominal pressure compresses inferior vena cava
Reduces venous return and drops left ventricular cardiac output
Systemic vascular resistance surges, elevating blood pressure

right.title: Pulmonary Mechanics Alterations
points: Diaphragm displaced cephalad, dropping FRC by up to 50 percent
Peak airway pressures rise, demanding volume-controlled PEEP
Peritoneal CO2 absorption requires increased minute ventilation
